GEN: Story runs from creation through the patriarchs (setting often placed in the second millennium BCE). Mainstream scholarship usually dates the finished Pentateuch, including Genesis in its present form, to the exilic or Persian period (6th–4th c. BCE), compiling older traditions. Traditional readings often stress an early Mosaic core with later editorial work.
JOB: The tale is set in a distant “land of Uz” with a wisdom frame; many readers associate its story setting with the patriarchal world after Genesis. Composition is widely placed in the 6th–4th c. BCE (exile/Persian era wisdom literature), though some argue for older poetic cores.
EXO: Narrates Moses, the plagues, and the exodus from Egypt (Late Bronze / Iron Age setting in the text). Critical study often assigns the present literary shape to 7th–5th c. BCE layers within the larger Pentateuchal tradition history; confessional scholarship often defends substantially earlier origins.
LEV: Laws and rituals tied to Sinai in the narrative. Like Exodus, its final compilation is commonly dated with the Pentateuch to the first millennium BCE, with debate between documentary models and alternative reconstructions.
NUM: Wilderness wanderings after Sinai. Textual layers are typically analyzed together with the Torah as post-monarchic editorial work framing older priestly and narrative material.
DEU: Moses’ speeches on the plains of Moab; central to the Deuteronomistic movement. Many scholars place a core in the late monarchy (7th c. BCE) with exilic expansions; others argue different stratigraphies.
JOS: Conquest and allotment of Canaan. The book in current form is often linked to 7th–6th c. BCE contexts in critical models, while maximalist historians debate how much reflects Iron Age memory.
JDG: Cycles of judges before the monarchy (Iron Age I setting). Final editing is frequently dated 7th–6th c. BCE alongside other Deuteronomistic material.
RUT: Story set in the judges period; themes of loyalty and David’s ancestry. The Hebrew book is often dated 6th–4th c. BCE; the Greek Ruth scroll can be later.
1SA: Samuel, Saul, and the rise of David (monarchy narrative). The Deuteronomistic History is often associated with Josianic (7th c.) and exilic editorial stages.
2SA: David’s reign and court history (including what became embedded source material for Kings/Chronicles). Same broad Deuteronomistic editorial framework as 1 Samuel.
PSA: Poems spanning many periods; superscriptions tie many psalms to David and later temple worship. Individual psalms may range 10th–4th c. BCE or beyond; the Psalter’s collection grew across centuries into the Second Temple era.
1KI: Solomon through the divided kingdom (9th–8th c. BCE events in the narrative). The book as we read it is usually seen as shaped before and during the exile within the Deuteronomistic History.
2KI: Continues through Assyrian conquest of Israel and Babylonian exile of Judah. Exilic 6th c. BCE editing is a common anchor for the history’s latest layers.
PRO: Mostly Solomonic attribution in headers; sayings may collect wisdom from monarchy through post-exilic times. Critical scholars often emphasize Persian or Hellenistic stages for major compilations.
ECC: Attributed to Qoheleth (“Teacher”); language and thought lead many scholars to 3rd c. BCE Hellenistic-era composition, though conservative readers propose earlier settings.
SNG: Love poetry; Solomonic title is traditional. Dates from 4th–3rd c. BCE are common in critical discussion, with wide uncertainty.
OBA: Short oracle against Edom; often tied to 6th c. BCE Jerusalem’s fall or slightly earlier Edomite conflict—dating is disputed.
JOL: Locust plague and day of the Lord; composition date highly debated (pre-exilic, exilic, or even Hellenistic proposals all appear in scholarship).
JON: Nineveh narrative; often placed post-exilic (5th–4th c. BCE) as reflective story rather than 8th-c. Assyrian reportage, though readings differ.
AMO: Ministry to northern Israel mid-8th c. BCE (under Jeroboam II) is the usual historical setting; the scroll may have been finalized later.
HOS: Prophesied in northern Israel 8th c. BCE; oracles likely collected and edited across the century into exile.
MIC: Contemporary of Isaiah in the late 8th c. BCE; chapters 4–7 especially reflect Assyrian-era Judah.
ISA: Chapters 1–39 largely 8th c. BCE Jerusalem; Second Isaiah (40–55) is widely dated to exilic Babylon (6th c. BCE); Third Isaiah (56–66) often post-exilic—a three-stage model is standard in critical introductions.
NAM: Nineveh’s fall (612 BCE context); book often placed 7th c. BCE or soon after.
HAB: Dialogue before Babylonian advance; commonly dated late 7th c. BCE.
ZEP: Before Josiah’s reform; late 7th c. BCE Judah is the usual setting.
JER: From Josiah’s reign through exile (late 7th–early 6th c. BCE). The scroll grew through Baruch-era collections and exilic supplements in many models.
LAM: Mourns Jerusalem’s fall (586 BCE setting); five poems often linked to 6th c. BCE though authorship debates continue.
EZK: Among exiles in Babylon; dated explicitly in the text to 6th c. BCE; critical scholarship generally agrees on an exilic core.
DAN: Court tales in 6th c. BCE setting; visions in 2nd c. BCE Greek persecution are the usual critical dating for the book’s final form, reflecting a long compositional history.
EZR: Return and temple rebuilding under Persian rule; text often placed 4th c. BCE alongside Chronicles-Ezra-Nehemiah editorial unity debates.
NEH: Wall rebuilding and reform; mid-5th c. BCE narrative setting with 4th c. BCE literary context common in scholarship.
EST: Persian court of Xerxes/Ahasuerus; 5th–4th c. BCE setting. Greek Esther additions are later; Hebrew Esther’s date is debated but usually Persian period.
HAG: Post-exile temple call; 520 BCE (Darius I) is explicit in the text.
ZEC: Visions and oracles from 520–518 BCE in the opening chapters; later chapters are often assigned to later 6th–5th c. BCE or separate hands.
MAL: Disputations in a restored community; often 5th c. BCE Persian-era Judah.
1CH: Retells Israel’s story from Adam through Saul, framing David. Most scholars date Chronicles-Ezra-Nehemiah compilation 4th–3rd c. BCE.
2CH: Solomon through exile and Cyrus’ edict; same late Persian / early Hellenistic compositional horizon as 1 Chronicles in mainstream models.
MAT: Jesus’ life and teaching; critical dating commonly AD 80–90 (post-temple) though some argue earlier 70s; traditional views favor apostolic eyewitness sources behind the text.
MRK: Often considered the first written Gospel; many scholars propose AD 65–73 around or just after the Jewish war, with debate on precision.
LUK: Two-volume work with Acts; often AD 80–90 (or slightly later) in critical consensus, with emphasis on orderly use of prior sources.
JHN: Distinct theological idiom; common critical range AD 90–110; some researchers explore earlier “signs source” layers.
ACT: Continuation of Luke; narrative reaches Paul’s Roman custody; composition usually paired with Luke late first century.
1TH: Among Paul’s earliest letters; often AD 50–51 from Corinth on Paul’s second journey.
2TH: Companion to 1 Thessalonians; many scholars accept Pauline authorship ~AD 50–52; a minority argue pseudepigraphy later.
GAL: Defense of Gentile inclusion without Torah markers; usually AD 53–55 (South Galatia) or mid-50s (North Galatia) depending on hypothesis.
1CO: Corinthian correspondence mid-50s AD from Ephesus on Paul’s third journey.
2CO: Often a composite of multiple letters; commonly AD 56–57 within the Corinthian archive.
ROM: Climactic letter on justification and Israel; AD 57 (Corinth/Cenchrea before Jerusalem trip) is widely accepted.
EPH: Many critical scholars date Ephesians AD 70–90 and debate Pauline authorship; traditional readers often place it with Paul’s Roman imprisonment ~AD 60–62.
PHP: Joy letter from prison; usually early 60s AD if Pauline imprisonment; similar debates as Ephesians/Colossians triad.
COL: Often grouped with Philemon and Ephesians as prison letters ~AD 60–62 in traditional chronologies; critical views vary on authorship and date.
1TI: Pastoral Epistles; critical scholarship often places them early second century with debate; traditional readers attribute them to Paul’s later 60s AD.
TIT: Church order on Crete; same Pastoral dating debates as 1 Timothy.
2TI: Paul’s “final” letter in the canon’s narrative; Pastoral composition questions mirror 1 Timothy/Titus.
PHM: Short slave-appeal from prison; ~AD 60–62 commonly if Colossian imprisonment context is accepted.
HEB: Anonymous sermon; dates from AD 60–95 proposed; pre-70 temple language is often noted, but Rome audience hints also appear—no consensus on author.
JAS: Wisdom moral exhortation; many scholars favor late first century (after Paul) or early second century; traditional James the Just as author is defended by some.
1PE: Comfort under suspicion; AD 62–64 (Nero’s Rome) is a frequent range, with Asia Minor audience.
2PE: Delayed parousia and false teachers; AD 125–150 is common among critical scholars who argue for second-century pseudepigraphy; traditional views defend Petrine authorship ~AD 64–68.
1JN: Community letter on love and christology; late first century Ephesus circle is a typical reconstruction.
2JN: Brief elder’s note; usually late first century with Johannine school theories.
3JN: Traveling teachers and hospitality; same Johannine horizon as 2 John.
JUD: Contend for the faith; late first or early second century is common, with parallels to Jewish pseudepigrapha.
REV: Apocalypse from John on Patmos; Domitian’s reign (~AD 95–96) is the traditional external attestation; some argue Neronian or earlier trauma contexts.
